questions.q: How does a catalyst increase the rate of a chemical reaction?
options: By increasing the temperature of the reactants.
By increasing the concentration of reactants.
By providing an alternative reaction mechanism with a lower activation energy.
By making the reaction more exothermic (more negative $\Delta H$).
questions.explain: A catalyst functions to accelerate reactions by providing an alternative reaction mechanism with a lower activation energy ($E_a$). It does not change $\Delta H$. Source: OpenStax 12.7 Catalysis.
questions.subject: Chemistry

questions.q: Which of the following best describes a **heterogeneous** catalyst?
options: A catalyst that is in the same phase as the reactants.
A catalyst that is present in a different phase (usually a solid) than the reactants.
A biological catalyst made of protein.
A catalyst that is consumed and then regenerated in the same phase.
questions.explain: A heterogeneous catalyst is a catalyst that is present in a different phase (usually a solid) than the reactants (often gas or liquid). Source: OpenStax 12.7 Catalysis.
questions.subject: Chemistry

questions.q: In the context of enzyme catalysis, what does the 'lock-and-key' model suggest?
options: The enzyme is flexible and changes shape to fit the substrate.
The molecular shape of the active site and substrate are complementary, fitting together perfectly.
The enzyme permanently bonds to the substrate.
Any substrate can fit into the enzyme's active site if it has enough energy.
questions.explain: The lock-and-key hypothesis suggests that the molecular shapes of the active site and substrate are complementary, fitting together like a key in a lock. (Contrast with Induced Fit). Source: OpenStax 12.7 Catalysis.
